label: 2-4 steps after a j at the start of the input (j as token 0 or 1)
explanation: Fires during the original-input phase (and occasionally the <DEL> step of short sequences) in sequences whose first or second original token is j, in a short window 2-4 steps after that j: t=2..4 when orig(0)=j, t=3..5 when orig(1)=j. The token being read at those steps does not matter. It never fires at t=0-1, almost never at t>=6, and essentially never in the copy phase. It is strongest when j comes first (82% of mass is in first_tok=j sequences), and strongest when the leading run contains several j tokens (e.g. j j j ...), with a peak about 2 steps after the last leading j. Activations decay over the next 1-2 steps. A j that first appears later in the sequence produces at most weak activation. Dev: P 0.77, R 0.87, mass recall 0.97.

issues: The core idea holds up: the feature is about j at orig(0) or orig(1). Sequences where neither of the first two tokens is j hold only 0.4% of activation mass. A j that first appears at position 2 gives almost nothing (P 0.002, mass 0.05%). Copy-phase firing is ~0.1% of mass, and t=0-1 never fire. Those claims check out.

The orig(1)=j window is wrong. It is t=3..4, not t=3..5. When orig(1)=j and orig(0)!=j (phase 0), precision is 0.81 at t=3 and 0.77 at t=4 but only 0.148 at t=5 (10674 steps predicted, mostly false positives). In the <DEL> phase it is 0.023 (5291 predicted, almost all false positives). This is a systematic false-positive class, not scattered noise, and the test misses list is dominated by it (e.g. 'r j f c <DEL>', 'u j w b <DEL>', 'n j r <DEL>').

The orig(0)=j window is the reverse problem: it is too short. orig(0)=j at t=5 in phase 0 is active with precision 0.51, recall 0.067 and 2.8% of mass. These are the main systematic misses on test (e.g. 'j h b l [j] ...', 'j t z z [p] ...').

So the windows are not '2-4 steps after the j' for both cases. When orig(0)=j the window is t=2..5 (2-5 steps after). When orig(1)=j it is t=3..4 (2-3 steps after). The firing is better described as a roughly fixed span of early positions, gated on j at the start, than as a symmetric offset from the j. The explanation's claim that false positives are 'mostly the window edges' admits the problem, but the predicate builds the wrong edges in.
The <DEL>-step claim only holds for orig(0)=j: precision 0.69 at phase 1 with t<=4. For orig(1)=j the <DEL> step almost never fires (P 0.023).
With the windows corrected, test F1 goes from 0.821 to 0.887 (P 0.858, R 0.918, mass recall 0.989).
